Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] TA4922 phishing lure themes (payroll/VAT/tax/HR) into EU recipients · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Atlas RAT anti-sandbox probes for Application Guard / CExecSvc / OS UUID · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] RomulusLoader-style unauthorized AnyDesk / SyncFuture install on EU endpoint · [LLM] TA4922 loader / Atlas RAT known SHA256 file write or execution · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] TA4922 C2 callback to Atlas RAT / RomulusLoader infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SilentRunLoader Python-based Chrome credential / cookie theft · [LLM] Atlas RAT operator-driven host shutdown / reboot impact
[LLM] TA4922 phishing lure themes (payroll/VAT/tax/HR) into EU recipients Delivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails using TA4922's localized phishing lures (payroll, tax-audit, VAT filing, government, invoice, HR) into Germany/Italy/UK/South Africa recipients, especially those containing URLs to the campaign's C2 domains. Article-specific because it pivots on the four-country target set + the named C2 hostnames. Rationale: Pivots on the four lure themes the article explicitly lists (payroll/VAT/tax/invoice/HR) localized to the named target countries (German + Italian translations included), correlated with the three pre-extracted C2 domains. Sentinel query uses OfficeActivity (no DeviceName column) since this is mailflow telemetry.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566.002 T1566.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
let LureRegex = @"(?i)(payroll|lohnabrechnung|gehaltsabrechnung|vat|umsatzsteuer|iva|tax\s*audit|steuerpr(ü|ue)fung|verifica\s*fiscale|invoice|rechnung|fattura|hr\s*notice|personalabteilung|compliance\s*notice|vat\s*filing)";
let C2Domains = dynamic(["aeya388.club","ws.ztts88.cyou","nwphotoblog.com"]);
let UrlMatches = EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where UrlDomain has_any (C2Domains)
| project NetworkMessageId, MatchedUrl = Url, MatchedDomain = UrlDomain;
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where EmailDirection =~ "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in~ ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where Subject matches regex LureRegex
     or NetworkMessageId in ((UrlMatches | project NetworkMessageId))
| join kind=leftouter UrlMatches on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, EmailLanguage, SenderIPv4, MatchedUrl, MatchedDomain, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
let LureRegex = @"(?i)(payroll|lohnabrechnung|gehaltsabrechnung|vat|umsatzsteuer|iva|tax\s*audit|steuerpr(ü|ue)fung|verifica\s*fiscale|invoice|rechnung|fattura|hr\s*notice|personalabteilung|compliance\s*notice)";
let C2Domains = dynamic(["aeya388.club","ws.ztts88.cyou","nwphotoblog.com"]);
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OfficeWorkload =~ "Exchange"

[LLM] TA4922 C2 callback to Atlas RAT / RomulusLoader infrastructure Command & Control High
Detects endpoint network egress to any of the five TA4922 C2 IPs or three C2 domains identified by Proofpoint, with the initiating process surfaced so analysts can pivot to the loader / RAT binary. Article-specific because it bolts directly to the pre-extracted IOC bundle. Rationale: Uses the five C2 IPs and three C2 domains pre-extracted from the Proofpoint IOC bundle. High-confidence atomic indicator match. Sentinel query uses CommonSecurityLog/DnsEvents/ImNetworkSession with their correct host-identifier columns (SourceHostName / Computer / DvcHostname) — no DeviceName references.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS

[LLM] Atlas RAT anti-sandbox probes for Application Guard / CExecSvc / OS UUID Exploitation Medium
Catches Atlas RAT's pre-execution environment fingerprint: registry reads of Microsoft Defender Application Guard keys, queries for the CExecSvc service, and reads of SMBIOS / OS UUID — all from a single short-lived process burst. Article-specific: Proofpoint explicitly enumerates these three checks. Rationale: Pivots on the three specific environment checks Proofpoint named (Application Guard registry keys, CExecSvc service, OS UUID via WMIC csproduct). The triple-probe pattern from one process is high-fidelity because legitimate sandbox-detection tooling is rare on user endpoints.
ATT&CKT1497.001 T1082 T1012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry
let AppGuardKeys = dynamic([@"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Hvsi", @"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\HVSI", @"SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CExecSvc"]);
let RegProbes = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryKeyOpened","RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any (AppGuardKeys) or RegistryKey has "CExecSvc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName;
let UuidProbes = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("csproduct","uuid"))
     or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Win32_ComputerSystemProduct","UUID"))
     or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Hvsi","CExecSvc","Application Guard"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, UuidProcessId = ProcessId, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256;
RegProbes
| join kind=inner UuidProbes on DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, Timestamp1)) <= 60
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RegistryKey, UuidCmdLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine1
| order by Timestamp desc
let AppGuardKeys = dynamic([@"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Hvsi", @"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\HVSI", @"SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CExecSvc"]);
let RegProbes = ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has_any (AppGuardKeys) or RegistryKey has "CExecSvc"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey;
let UuidProbes = SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("csproduct","uuid"))
     or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Win32_ComputerSystemProduct","UUID"))
     or (NewProcessName endswith "\\reg.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("Hvsi","CExecSvc","Application Guard"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProbeProcessName = NewProcessName, ProbeCmd = CommandLine, ParentProcessName;
RegProbes
| join kind=inner (UuidProbes) on $left.DvcHostname == $right.Computer
| where abs(datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, TimeGenerated1)) <= 60
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, ProbeProcessName, ProbeCmd
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon ((@EventID:13 AND (@TargetObject:(*\Hvsi* OR *\HVSI* OR *\hvsi* OR *CExecSvc* OR *cexecsvc* OR *"Application Guard"*))) OR (@EventID:1 AND @CommandLine:(*csproduct* OR *Win32_ComputerSystemProduct* OR *"uuid"* OR *Hvsi* OR *CExecSvc*)))
(#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate OR #event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2)
| (RegObjectName=/(Hvsi|CExecSvc|Application Guard)/i OR CommandLine=/(csproduct|Win32_ComputerSystemProduct|Hvsi|CExecSvc|Application Guard|\buuid\b)/i)
| ImageFileName=/(wmic|reg|powershell|pwsh|cmd)\.exe$/i OR ContextImageFileName=/(wmic|reg|powershell|pwsh|cmd)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName], function=[count(), collect([CommandLine, RegObjectName])])
| _count > 1

[LLM] SilentRunLoader Python-based Chrome credential / cookie theft Actions on Objectives High
Detects non-Chrome processes (especially python.exe, py.exe, pythonw.exe, or unsigned LOLBins) opening Chrome's Login Data, Cookies, Web Data, or Local State files — the exact targeting Proofpoint attributes to SilentRunLoader. Pivots on the Python-loader fingerprint rather than a generic credential-dumper template. Rationale: Pivots on the exact targeting Proofpoint named (Chrome credentials, cookies, browsing data) plus SilentRunLoader's Python runtime fingerprint. Chrome's User Data files are read only by Chrome / Google Updater in normal operation, so python.exe touching them is a high-confidence stealer signal.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileOpened")
| where FolderPath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Login Data-journal","Cookies","Cookies-journal","Web Data","Local State","Network\\Cookies")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","GoogleUpdateComRegisterShell64.exe","explorer.exe","backupd.exe")
         and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "Google")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Google\Chrome\User Data\"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Login Data-journal","Cookies","Cookies-journal","Web Data","Local State")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","py.exe","python3.exe")
     or (ActingProcessName !has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","GoogleUpdate.exe","explorer.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] RomulusLoader-style unauthorized AnyDesk / SyncFuture install on EU endpoint Installation High
Detects fresh installs or first-time launches of AnyDesk and SyncFuture binaries — the RMM combo TA4922 weaponizes via RomulusLoader — on hosts that have never run them before. Pivots on SyncFuture (highly unusual outside Chinese deployments) and on AnyDesk launched by a non-installer parent. Rationale: SyncFuture is explicitly called out as a China-popular RMM that Proofpoint found on German victim hosts — its mere presence outside APAC is anomalous. AnyDesk on a first-seen-per-host basis catches the RomulusLoader handoff without alerting on routine vendor RMM use.
ATT&CKT1219 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let Baseline = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp between (ago(90d) .. ago(14d))
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","SyncFuture.exe","SyncFutureSetup.exe")
| summarize by DeviceName, FileName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","SyncFuture.exe","SyncFutureSetup.exe")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DeviceName, FileName
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","explorer.exe","AnyDesk.exe")
     or FileName in~ ("SyncFuture.exe","SyncFutureSetup.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let Baseline = SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(14d))
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\AnyDesk.exe","\\SyncFuture.exe","\\SyncFutureSetup.exe")
| summarize by Computer, NewProcessName;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\AnyDesk.exe","\\SyncFuture.exe","\\SyncFutureSetup.exe")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on Computer, NewProcessName
| where ParentProcessName !has_any ("\\msiexec.exe","\\explorer.exe","\\AnyDesk.exe")
     or NewProcessName has_any ("\\SyncFuture.exe","\\SyncFutureSetup.exe")

[LLM] Atlas RAT operator-driven host shutdown / reboot impact Actions on Objectives Medium
Catches the article's stated Atlas RAT impact capability: operator-triggered system shutdown/reboot. Correlates Windows shutdown/reboot events with a recent C2 connection from the same host so legitimate WSUS / GPO reboots don't drown the signal. Rationale: Article explicitly lists 'System shutdown/reboot commands' as an Atlas RAT capability. The C2-correlation join (shutdown within 4h of a beacon to the listed IOC IPs/domains) is what differentiates this from WSUS/GPO-driven reboots, which dominate raw 1074/6006/6008 volume.
ATT&CKT1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let C2IPs = dynamic(["206.238.115.58","154.211.86.110","43.156.77.97","103.214.172.33","18.139.83.110"]);
let C2Domains = dynamic(["aeya388.club","ws.ztts88.cyou","nwphotoblog.com"]);
let C2Hosts = DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2IPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
| project C2Time = Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl;
let Shutdowns = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("shutdown.exe","logoff.exe")
     or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Restart-Computer","Stop-Computer"))
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","taskhostw.exe","sihost.exe","wuauclt.exe","MsMpEng.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","services.exe","OfficeClickToRun.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256;
Shutdowns

| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Jupyter Enterprise Gateway /api/kernels POST with KERNEL_* YAML-injection payload · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-44182: Jupyter Enterprise Gateway: Kubernetes Manifes
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Privileged or root pod created by Jupyter Enterprise Gateway ServiceAccount
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] Jupyter Enterprise Gateway /api/kernels POST with KERNEL_* YAML-injection payload Exploitation Medium
Hunts for HTTP POSTs to the Jupyter Enterprise Gateway `/api/kernels` endpoint whose body carries `KERNEL_WORKING_DIR`, `KERNEL_POD_NAME`, `KERNEL_NAMESPACE` or other `KERNEL_*` env values containing YAML-injection markers (`---`, `...`, embedded `securityContext`, `runAsUser`, `privileged`). This is the exact CVE-2026-44182 exploit shape — the unsanitised env-var is interpolated into the Jinja2 pod manifest at kernel-pod.yaml.j2 line 77 and lets the caller overwrite or append Kubernetes resources. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit primitive from the GHSA PoC: a POST to /api/kernels carrying KERNEL_WORKING_DIR/KERNEL_POD_NAME/KERNEL_NAMESPACE whose value embeds a YAML breakout (`\n# INJECTION\n securityContext:\n runAsUser: 0` or `...\n---\napiVersion: v1\nkind: Pod`). The Jinja2 line referenced (kernel-pod.yaml.j2#L77) and the launch_kubernetes.py uppercase→lowercase conversion (lines 130-137) confirm these are the only attacker-controlled fields. No second-source corroboration searched — single advisory CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cfw7-6c5v-2wjq
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1611
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// Endpoint-tier visibility only — looks for outbound connections from a host to the EG service
// where the EG ingress is reachable internally; pair with WAF/ingress body inspection in Sentinel.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (31529, 8888, 8889, 8443)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/kernels" or AdditionalFields has "/api/kernels"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Detects KERNEL_* env-var with YAML-injection markers in EG application syslog or WAF body logs.
// CommonSecurityLog does NOT carry DeviceName — use DestinationHostName / SourceIP for host pivots.
let InjectionMarkers = @"(?i)KERNEL_[A-Z_]+[^\n]{0,200}(---|\.\.\.|securityContext|runAsUser|runAsGroup|fsGroup|privileged\s*:\s*true)";
union isfuzzy=true
(
  Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ProcessName has_any ("enterprise_gateway", "enterprise-gateway", "jupyter") or SyslogMessage has "/api/kernels"
  | where SyslogMessage matches regex InjectionMarkers
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="Syslog", Host=Computer, HostName, ProcessName, Evidence=SyslogMessage
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has "/api/kernels" and RequestMethod =~ "POST"
  | where Message matches regex InjectionMarkers or DeviceCustomString1 matches regex InjectionMarkers or AdditionalExtensions matches regex InjectionMarkers
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="WAF/Proxy", Host=DestinationHostName, SourceIP=SourceIP, ProcessName=DeviceProduct, Evidence=coalesce(Message, DeviceCustomString1, AdditionalExtensions)
),
(
  W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csUriStem == "/api/kernels" and csMethod =~ "POST"
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="IIS", Host=Computer, SourceIP=cIP, ProcessName="w3wp", Evidence=strcat(csMethod, " ", csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery)
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:kubernetes.audit @verb:create @objectRef.resource:pods @user.username:*enterprise-gateway* (@requestObject.spec.containers.workingDir:(*---* OR *...* OR *securityContext* OR *runAsUser* OR *privileged*) OR @requestObject.metadata.name:(*---* OR *...*))) OR (source:nginx.access @http.method:POST @http.url_details.path:/api/kernels @http.request.body:(*KERNEL_* AND (*---* OR *securityContext* OR *runAsUser* OR "privileged: true")))

[LLM] Privileged or root pod created by Jupyter Enterprise Gateway ServiceAccount Installation High
Detects the Kubernetes-API-server-side effect of CVE-2026-44182: a Pod created by the enterprise-gateway ServiceAccount whose spec contains `privileged: true`, `runAsUser: 0`, `runAsGroup: 0`, a `hostPath` mount, or `hostNetwork: true`. EG should only ever spawn unprivileged kernel pods running as uid 1000 (jovyan); any privileged spec from this SA is the post-injection footprint. Rationale: Anchors on the EG-default identity (the `enterprise-gateway` ServiceAccount, see Helm chart) and the article-stated effects: the PoC explicitly produces pods with `privileged:true, runAsUser:0, runAsGroup:0` and notes the impact extends to arbitrary `hostPath` mounts. Normal EG kernel pods run as `uid=1000(jovyan)` per the rendered template — any privileged/root spec from this SA is the injection footprint, not noise. Only the original GHSA cross-checked. [LLM] Jinja2 SSTI payload to Jupyter Enterprise Gateway /api/kernels (CVE-2026-44181) Exploitation High
Hunts for HTTP POST requests targeting Jupyter Enterprise Gateway's /api/kernels endpoint carrying a Jinja2 server-side template injection payload in KERNEL_POD_NAME / KERNEL_WORKING_DIR / KERNEL_NAMESPACE fields. Specifically pivots on the Python sandbox-escape gadgets (cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen, __subclasses__, __builtins__) that the PoC and any real-world weaponization must include to reach OS-command execution. Rationale: All keywords (`/api/kernels`, `KERNEL_POD_NAME`, `KERNEL_WORKING_DIR`, `KERNEL_NAMESPACE`, `{{`, `cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen`, `__subclasses__`) are taken verbatim from the GHSA PoC. The combination of an EG endpoint URL plus Jinja2 mustache markers plus Python globals-walk gadgets has essentially zero benign explanation. Defender XDR cannot inspect inbound HTTP bodies, so defender_kql is empty by design; Falcon FDR likewise does not ship raw HTTP body content. CloudWatch is non-applicable (not AWS-specific telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49j-v924-fx9w • https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/Python.md
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006

| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/kernels"
| where Message has_any ("KERNEL_POD_NAME", "KERNEL_WORKING_DIR", "KERNEL_NAMESPACE")
| where Message has "{{"
| where Message has_any ("__globals__", "__class__", "__mro__", "__subclasses__", "__builtins__", "cycler.__init__", "os.popen", "os.system", "subprocess", "__import__", "popen")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Enterprise Gateway service account creates privileged / hostPath / RBAC-escalating pod (CVE-2026-44181 post-exploit) Actions on Objectives High
Hunts for Kubernetes API actions by the Jupyter Enterprise Gateway service account that fall outside its legitimate role of launching kernel pods: creating a pod with privileged securityContext, hostPath / hostNetwork / hostPID, or creating/updating rolebindings, clusterrolebindings, or reading cluster secrets. These are the textbook pivots after stealing the EG SA token via SSTI RCE, as the GHSA explicitly notes. Rationale: The GHSA explicitly enumerates the Enterprise Gateway SA's RBAC — including `pods [create]`, `secrets [get watch list]`, `rolebindings [create]` — and explicitly names the attacker's next step (schedule a privileged pod or hostPath-volume pod for cluster takeover). The detection ties three article-specific anchors together: actor identity (`enterprise-gateway` in the SA username), action verb (create/update on pods/rolebindings/secrets), and payload shape (`privileged:true`, `hostPath`, `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`) — the legitimate kernel-launcher YAML never includes any of those. Falcon LogScale is left empty because FDR does not ship K8s audit; Defender Advanced Hunting likewise has no K8s-audit table. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49j-v924-fx9w • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/152c20f162f2fab700c04c8830ebf8c1e2e2217a/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2

[LLM] Enterprise Gateway python container spawns shell or reads K8s service-account token (CVE-2026-44181 RCE) Installation High
Hunts for the on-host signal of the SSTI RCE landing inside the Jupyter Enterprise Gateway pod: a python interpreter spawning a shell, recon binary, or curl/wget, or any process reading /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. The article's PoC uses `cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('hostname')` — `os.popen` results in a python→sh→hostname process tree that is otherwise unheard-of for the EG service. Rationale: The PoC payload `cycler.__init__.__globals__.os.popen("hostname").read()` proves the exact process-tree shape the detection targets: python (the Enterprise Gateway service) → sh -c → hostname. The article also explicitly names theft of the Kubernetes service-account token (`/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`) as the attacker objective, so we additionally pivot on any python-parented process referencing that path. Host-scope filters (`enterprise-gateway` in hostname / pod name / container image) keep the signal tight to the vulnerable workload rather than every python process in the fleet. CloudWatch is empty (not CloudTrail/VPC-flow telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49j-v924-fx9w • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/152c20f162f2fab700c04c8830ebf8c1e2e2217a/enterprise_gateway/services/processproxies/k8s.py#L219-L247

[LLM] Jupyter Enterprise Gateway /api/kernels POST with KERNEL_UID/GID body (CVE-2026-44180) Exploitation Medium
Hunts inbound POST requests to /api/kernels on the Enterprise Gateway service that supply KERNEL_UID or KERNEL_GID in the JSON body — the attack surface used to exploit the prohibited-UID/GID whitespace bypass described in CVE-2026-44180. Most production workloads call /api/kernels without explicitly setting these env keys, so unsolicited UID/GID-bearing requests are high-signal. Rationale: Anchors on the exact attack-surface URL '/api/kernels' and HTTP POST method from the PoC. Body content (the '0 ' bypass payload) rarely makes it into access logs, so this UC is a coarse hunting pivot — pair with UC2 (K8s audit on runAsUser=0) for ground truth. Cross-checked GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 and Jupyter Enterprise Gateway upstream docs (jupyter-enterprise-gateway.readthedocs.io kernel-envs). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 • https://jupyter-enterprise-gateway.readthedocs.io/en/latest/users/kernel-envs.html • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/main/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2

[LLM] Enterprise Gateway service account creates Jupyter kernel pod as root (CVE-2026-44180 outcome) Exploitation High
Detects the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-44180: a Kubernetes pod-create call whose service account belongs to enterprise-gateway and whose resolved PodSpec has runAsUser=0 or runAsGroup=0. Default kernel pods run as jovyan (1000:100); any kernel-* pod created with root UID/GID is either the documented bypass or a misconfiguration that should never reach production. Rationale: Article confirms the default kernel pod runs as uid=1000(jovyan) gid=100(users) — any kernel pod from the enterprise-gateway SA with runAsUser=0 is exactly the bypass outcome (Jinja2 int-coerces '0 '→0 even when EG_PROHIBITED_UIDS rejects '0'). Cross-referenced the kernel-pod.yaml.j2 template at jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway main branch (where securityContext.runAsUser is templated from KERNEL_UID). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/main/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2 • https://jupyter-enterprise-gateway.readthedocs.io/en/latest/users/kernel-envs.html

[LLM] Jupyter kernel pod created with hostPath volume by enterprise-gateway SA Actions on Objectives High
Detects the container-escape vector named in the advisory: a kernel pod from the enterprise-gateway service account that mounts a hostPath volume — especially sensitive worker-node paths (/, /etc, /var/spool/cron, /root, /home, /var/run/docker.sock). Combined with the root UID bypass (UC2), this is the path to crontab-driven node compromise the PoC describes. Rationale: The advisory explicitly names the escape recipe: 'use a hostPath R/W volume mount, use this UID/GID bypass to run as root, and then gain code execution in the underlying worker node by creating a crontab entry'. Kernel pods normally do not need hostPath at all — the default kernel-pod.yaml.j2 ships with only emptyDir-style mounts. Any hostPath volume on a kernel-* pod from the EG SA is article-defined-malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 • https://github.com/jupyter-server/enterprise_gateway/blob/main/etc/kernel-launchers/kubernetes/scripts/kernel-pod.yaml.j2
ATT&CKT1611 T1610
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb == "create"
| where tostring(ObjectRef) has "\"resource\":\"pods\""
| where tostring(User) has "enterprise-gateway" or Username has "enterprise-gateway"
| extend req = todynamic(tostring(RequestObject))
| extend podName = tostring(req.metadata.name)
| extend volumes = req.spec.volumes
| mv-expand v = volumes
| extend hostPath = tostring(v.hostPath.path)
| where isnotempty(hostPath)
| extend sensitive = iff(hostPath in ("/", "/etc", "/root", "/home", "/var/spool/cron", "/var/run/docker.sock", "/var/lib/kubelet", "/proc")
                          or hostPath startswith "/etc/"
                          or hostPath startswith "/var/spool/cron"
                          or hostPath startswith "/root/", "sensitive", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, podName, hostPath, sensitive, User, AuditId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cron/persistence file written on Kubernetes worker node from container runtime context Installation Medium
Detects creation or modification of /etc/cron* or /var/spool/cron/* files on Kubernetes worker nodes — the article's explicit post-escape persistence vector after the CVE-2026-44180 UID bypass + hostPath mount. Kernel pods exist to run user code, not to schedule host-level cron jobs; any cron-file write on a worker node is investigation-worthy. Rationale: Article PoC explicitly recommends 'creating a crontab entry in the mounted host file system' as the worker-node escape outcome. Filters specifically on container-runtime-spawned writes (runc / containerd-shim) because legitimate cron edits on a K8s worker should come from configuration-management agents (cloud-init, Ansible, Puppet) or package installs — not from runc. Cross-checked the article's mount-namespace escape pattern against MITRE T1611 / T1053.003. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611/
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath startswith "/etc/cron."
     or FolderPath == "/var/spool/cron"
     or FolderPath startswith "/var/spool/cron/"
     or (FolderPath == "/etc" and FileName in ("crontab","anacrontab"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, MachineGroup, AdditionalFields) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| where OSPlatform in ("Linux","Ubuntu","RedHat","CentOS","Debian","SUSE")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/run/containerd","/var/lib/docker","/var/lib/containerd","/usr/bin/runc","/usr/sbin/runc")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","crun","kata-runtime")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","crun")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/cron.weekly/","/etc/cron.monthly/","/var/spool/cron/")
     or TargetFilePath in ("/etc/crontab","/etc/anacrontab")
| extend ParentIsRuntime = ActingProcessName has_any ("runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2","crun","kata-runtime")
| where ParentIsRuntime or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/run/containerd","/var/lib/containerd","/var/lib/docker")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Cron Persistence Written from Container Runtime Context on K8s Worker
id: 8c2f1a47-d931-4e58-92a6-1f7b3c4d2e95
description: Detects writes to host cron paths on Kubernetes worker nodes whose initiating process is the container runtime (runc / containerd-shim) — a post-escape persistence step described in CVE-2026-44180 (Jupyter Enterprise Gateway hostPath + root-UID bypass).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chq7-94j8-cj28
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.t1053.003
  - attack.t1611
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.privilege_escalation
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|startswith:
      - '/etc/cron.d/'
      - '/etc/cron.daily/'
      - '/etc/cron.hourly/'
      - '/etc/cron.weekly/'
      - '/etc/cron.monthly/'
      - '/var/spool/cron/'
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename:
      - '/etc/crontab'
      - '/etc/anacrontab'
  selection_runtime:
    Image|contains:
      - 'runc'
      - 'containerd-shim'
      - 'crun'
      - 'kata-runtime'
  condition: (selection_path or selection_file) and selection_runtime
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) (@file.path:/etc/cron.d/* OR @file.path:/etc/cron.daily/* OR @file.path:/etc/cron.hourly/* OR @file.path:/etc/cron.weekly/* OR @file.path:/etc/cron.monthly/* OR @file.path:/var/spool/cron/* OR @file.path:/etc/crontab OR @file.path:/etc/anacrontab) (@process.executable.path:*runc* OR @process.executable.path:*containerd-shim* OR @process.executable.path:*crun* OR @process.command_line:*\/run\/containerd*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/^\/(etc\/(cron(tab|\.(d|daily|hourly|weekly|monthly))|anacrontab)|var\/spool\/cron)/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(runc|containerd-shim|crun|kata-runtime)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| count > 0
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count, values(Filesystem.process_name) as procs, values(Filesystem.user) as users from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path IN ("/etc/crontab","/etc/anacrontab") OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.d/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.daily/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.hourly/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.weekly/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.monthly/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/var/spool/cron/*") Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","written") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search dest IN ("*worker*","*node*","*k8s*","*kube*") OR procs IN ("runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2") | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Filesystem.process_name) as procs, values(Filesystem.user) as users from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path IN ("/etc/crontab","/etc/anacrontab") OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.d/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.daily/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.hourly/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.weekly/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/etc/cron.monthly/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/var/spool/cron/*") Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","written") by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.file_path, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search dest IN ("*worker*","*node*","*k8s*","*kube*") OR procs IN ("runc","containerd-shim","containerd-shim-runc-v2") | sort - _time
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-44180")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-44180")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-44180")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-44180")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

The U.S. sanctions Nobitex crypto exchange used by ransomware

BleepingComputer
2026-06-03 5 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced sanctions against Nobitex, Iran's largest cryptocurrency exchange, for facilitating payments related to terrorist activities. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1486
DomainsNobitex.ir Wallex.ir Bitcoin.ir Rumzinex.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to OFAC-sanctioned Iranian crypto exchanges (Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin, Ramzinex) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Network egress to OFAC-sanctioned Iranian crypto exchanges (Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin, Ramzinex) Command & Control High
Hunts for DNS / HTTP / proxy traffic from corporate endpoints to the four Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges (Nobitex.ir, Wallex.ir, Bitpin.ir, Ramzinex.com) designated by OFAC on 2026-06-03 under the 'Economic Fury' campaign. Any U.S.-jurisdiction host reaching these domains creates an immediate sanctions-compliance event, and may also surface IRGC-affiliated ransomware operators routing payments through Nobitex. Rationale: Uses the four exchange domains pre-extracted from the article (Nobitex.ir, Wallex.ir, Bitpin.ir, Ramzinex.com — note article typo 'Rumzinex.com' is also covered). These are not generic threat-hunting indicators — they map to a specific OFAC SDN designation issued 2026-06-03 under the 'Economic Fury' campaign, so any U.S.-jurisdiction contact is itself the violation. Cross-checked: Treasury press release referenced in body, and Chainalysis 2025 Iran crypto ecosystem figures (~$7.8B inflow, Nobitex >50%) used to scope criticality. The article also cites the 2025 Predatory Sparrow breach of Nobitex, confirming the exchange's role as IRGC-linked ransomware payment infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/recent-actions • https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/iran-crypto-ecosystem-2025/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1657
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let SanctionedDomains = dynamic(["nobitex.ir","wallex.ir","bitpin.ir","ramzinex.com","rumzinex.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (SanctionedDomains)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let SanctionedDomains = dynamic(["nobitex.ir","wallex.ir","bitpin.ir","ramzinex.com","rumzinex.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
  ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (SanctionedDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = coalesce(SrcHostname, DvcHostname), SrcIp = SrcIpAddr, User = SrcUsername, Indicator = DnsQuery, Source = "DNS"
),
(
  ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Url has_any (SanctionedDomains) or HttpHostName has_any (SanctionedDomains) or DstHostname has_any (SanctionedDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = coalesce(SrcHostname, DvcHostname), SrcIp = SrcIpAddr, User = SrcUsername, Indicator = coalesce(Url, HttpHostName, DstHostname), Source = "Web"
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has_any (SanctionedDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (SanctionedDomains) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (SanctionedDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, SrcIp = SourceIP, User = SourceUserName, Indicator = coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain), Source = "Proxy"
),
(
  DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Name has_any (SanctionedDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, SrcIp = ClientIP, User = "", Indicator = Name, Source = "WinDNS"
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS / Web Connection to OFAC-Sanctioned Iranian Crypto Exchange (2026 Economic Fury)
id: 7c5d2f1b-9a83-4e6a-8f2d-1c5b9f3e7a4d
description: Detects DNS resolution or web traffic to the four Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges (Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin, Ramzinex) designated by OFAC on 2026-06-03 for facilitating IRGC-linked ransomware payments and sanctions evasion. Any contact from a U.S.-jurisdiction host is a sanctions-compliance event.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-us-sanctions-nobitex-crypto-exchange-used-by-ransomware/
  - https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/recent-actions
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1071.004
  - attack.t1657
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith:
      - nobitex.ir
      - wallex.ir
      - bitpin.ir
      - ramzinex.com
      - rumzinex.com
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Sanctioned-trade compliance / treasury research teams with documented business need
  - Threat intelligence researchers actively profiling Iranian crypto infrastructure
  - Security-vendor crawlers (VirusTotal, urlscan, abuse.ch) operating from corporate IP space
level: high
(@dns.question.name:(*nobitex.ir OR *wallex.ir OR *bitpin.ir OR *ramzinex.com OR *rumzinex.com) OR @network.destination.domain:(nobitex.ir OR wallex.ir OR bitpin.ir OR ramzinex.com OR rumzinex.com) OR @http.url_details.host:(nobitex.ir OR wallex.ir OR bitpin.ir OR ramzinex.com OR rumzinex.com) OR @QueryName:(*nobitex.ir OR *wallex.ir OR *bitpin.ir OR *ramzinex.com OR *rumzinex.com) OR @DestinationHostname:(*nobitex.ir OR *wallex.ir OR *bitpin.ir OR *ramzinex.com OR *rumzinex.com))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)(nobitex\.ir|wallex\.ir|bitpin\.ir|ramzinex\.com|rumzinex\.com)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(as=Hits), min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=LastSeen)])
| sort(LastSeen, order=desc)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*nobitex.ir*","*wallex.ir*","*bitpin.ir*","*ramzinex.com*","*rumzinex.com*") OR Web.dest IN ("*nobitex.ir","*wallex.ir","*bitpin.ir","*ramzinex.com","*rumzinex.com")) by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.http_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | append [ | tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("*nobitex.ir","*wallex.ir","*bitpin.ir","*ramzinex.com","*rumzinex.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | rename query as dest ] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url IN ("*nobitex.ir*","*wallex.ir*","*bitpin.ir*","*ramzinex.com*","*rumzinex.com*") OR Web.dest IN ("*nobitex.ir","*wallex.ir","*bitpin.ir","*ramzinex.com","*rumzinex.com")) by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.http_method | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | append [ | tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("*nobitex.ir","*wallex.ir","*bitpin.ir","*ramzinex.com","*rumzinex.com") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | rename query as dest ] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:

    - attack.credential-access

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")

[LLM] Vulnerable HTTP/2 server inventory (CVE-2026-49975 — nginx/mod_http2/Envoy/IIS) Weaponization High
Surfaces hosts running HTTP/2-capable web servers at versions the Calif researchers proved vulnerable to the HTTP/2 Bomb (nginx pre-1.29.8, Apache httpd with mod_http2 < 2.0.41, Envoy 1.37.2, and IIS on Windows Server 2025 where no patch yet exists). Inventory-based hunt that prioritises patching/HTTP-2-disable work and identifies the attack surface for the follow-up runtime detections. Rationale: Pivots on CveId == CVE-2026-49975 (the assigned identifier from the Apache disclosure) plus the exact vulnerable build strings the article names (nginx 1.29.7, mod_http2 < 2.0.41, Envoy 1.37.2, IIS on Windows Server 2025). Joining DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing focuses triage on hosts the article notes are most exposed — CDN-fronted estates are 'more difficult to target'. Cross-checked against Tenable's CVE record and the upstream nginx commit adding max_headers. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-49975 • https://github.com/nginx/nginx/commit/365694160a85229a7cb006738de9260d49ff5fa2 • https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/790

[LLM] HTTP/2 Bomb stall signature — long-hung HTTP/2 requests with near-zero response bytes Command & Control Medium
Detects the zero-window flow-control hold half of the HTTP/2 Bomb: the server has allocated memory but never emits a response because the client advertises a zero-byte WINDOW. On the wire this shows up as small numbers of inbound HTTP/2 requests from a single source IP that each persist for tens of seconds while the server returns almost no bytes. Targets IIS / nginx / Apache / Envoy access logs and inbound network telemetry. Rationale: Encodes the exact wire signature the article describes: 'requests are never fully completed, and the allocated memory keeps growing' via zero-byte WINDOW + tiny WINDOW_UPDATE responses. TimeTaken ≥ 20s with scBytes ≤ 1024 captures Apache/Envoy 32-GB-in-20s and IIS 64-GB-in-45s profiles. Few-but-long (HungReqs ≥ 3) — not a flood — matches Calif's 'single-client' claim. Cross-checked against the Calif technical write-up (blog.calif.io) and SecurityWeek's reproduction summary. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://www.securityweek.com/http-2-bomb-exploit-knocks-web-servers-offline-in-seconds/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-http2-bomb-vulnerability-allows.html
ATT&CKT1499.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
// HTTP/2 Bomb stall signature — multiple held inbound HTTP/2 connections from a single source
let WebProcs = dynamic(["nginx.exe","httpd.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","iisexpress.exe","apache2","nginx","httpd"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ActionType =~ "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (443, 8443, 80)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (WebProcs)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"        // ignore intra-DC health checks
| summarize ConnCount       = count(),
            DistinctRemotePorts = dcount(RemotePort),
            FirstConn        = min(Timestamp),
            LastConn         = max(Timestamp),
            HoldSeconds      = datetime_diff('second', max(Timestamp), min(Timestamp))
        by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where ConnCount >= 20 and HoldSeconds >= 20    // 20+ simultaneous inbound h2 conns held ≥20s — matches Apache/Envoy 32GB-in-20s profile
| project FirstConn, LastConn, DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, ConnCount, DistinctRemotePorts, HoldSeconds
| order by ConnCount desc
// HTTP/2 Bomb stall — IIS/web access logs showing held requests with near-zero response
let IISHung =
    W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where TimeTaken >= 20000           // ≥20s — article: 32GB consumed in ~20s on Apache/Envoy
    | where scBytes  <= 1024             // server emitted no real response body
    | where csMethod !in~ ("PUT","POST") or csBytes < 65536   // exclude legitimate slow large uploads
    | summarize HungReqs = count(),
                DistinctUris = dcount(csUriStem),
                TotalHoldMs = sum(TimeTaken),
                MaxHoldMs   = max(TimeTaken),
                SampleAgent = any(csUserAgent),
                FirstSeen   = min(TimeGenerated),
                LastSeen    = max(TimeGenerated)
            by cIP, sSiteName, Computer
    | where HungReqs >= 3                // bomb is FEW long streams, not a flood
    | project FirstSeen, LastSeen, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, HungReqs, DistinctUris, MaxHoldMs, TotalHoldMs, SampleAgent;
let AsimHung =
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where NetworkDuration >= 20000
    | where HttpResponseBodyBytes <= 1024
    | summarize HungReqs = count(),
                TotalHoldMs = sum(NetworkDuration),
                MaxHoldMs   = max(NetworkDuration),
                DistinctUris = dcount(Url),
                FirstSeen   = min(TimeGenerated),
                LastSeen    = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname
    | where HungReqs >= 3
    | project FirstSeen, LastSeen, Computer=DvcHostname, sSiteName="", cIP=SrcIpAddr, HungReqs, DistinctUris, MaxHoldMs, TotalHoldMs, SampleAgent="";
union IISHung, AsimHung
| order by MaxHoldMs desc

fields @timestamp, client_ip, target_processing_time, request_processing_time, response_processing_time, sent_bytes, received_bytes, request_url, elb_status_code, protocol
| filter protocol = "HTTP/2"

[LLM] Web-tier worker crash / OOM storm following HTTP/2 Bomb memory exhaustion Actions on Objectives High
Detects the impact phase: rapid worker-process recycles or OOM-killer events on hosts running nginx, Apache httpd, IIS (w3wp.exe), or Envoy. The HTTP/2 Bomb causes 32–64 GB of RAM to be consumed in 10–45 seconds; on Linux this triggers oom-killer; on Windows IIS this triggers Application Pool crash-recycles and Application Error 1000 events naming w3wp.exe. Designed to fire even if the on-wire UC2 missed the request shape. Rationale: Built directly on the article's impact description — 32–64 GB RAM exhaustion in 10–45 seconds. On Linux this surfaces as oom-killer entries naming nginx/httpd/envoy in Syslog; on Windows IIS the bomb crash-loops the application pool, producing Application Error 1000 events naming w3wp.exe plus rapid 4688 NewProcessName=w3wp.exe spawns. Pivots on web-server binary names from the article's tested versions. Cross-checked against the Calif technical write-up and the oss-sec disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/790 • https://gbhackers.com/http-2-bomb-remote-dos-exploit/
ATT&CKT1499.003 T1499.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
// HTTP/2 Bomb impact — web worker restart storm (process pool churn from OOM)
let WebProcs = dynamic(["nginx.exe","httpd.exe","apache2","httpd","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","nginx"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where FileName in~ WebProcs or FileName has_any (WebProcs)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize SpawnCount    = count(),
            DistinctPids  = dcount(ProcessId),
            FirstSpawn    = min(Timestamp),
            LastSpawn     = max(Timestamp),
            SampleParent  = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            SampleCmd     = any(ProcessCommandLine)
        by DeviceName, FileName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where SpawnCount >= 10                           // 10 worker (re)starts in 5 min — well above normal recycle rate
| extend StormWindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastSpawn, FirstSpawn)
| project FirstSpawn, LastSpawn, StormWindowSec, DeviceName, FileName, SpawnCount, DistinctPids, SampleParent, SampleCmd
| order by SpawnCount desc
// HTTP/2 Bomb impact — OOM-killer (Linux) and Application Error 1000 (Windows IIS) targeting web workers
let LookbackHours = 1h;
let LinuxOOM =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where SyslogMessage has "oom-killer" or (SyslogMessage has "Out of memory" and SyslogMessage has "Killed process")
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("nginx","httpd","apache2","envoy")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName="oom-killer", Detail=SyslogMessage, Platform="Linux";
let WinIISCrash =
    Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where EventID == 1000 and Source has "Application Error"
    | where RenderedDescription has_any ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","envoy.exe")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName="Application Error 1000", Detail=RenderedDescription, Platform="Windows";
let WinWorkerStorm =
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\w3wp.exe","\\nginx.exe","\\httpd.exe","\\envoy.exe")
    | summarize Spawns=count(), arg_min(TimeGenerated, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName) by Computer, NewProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
    | where Spawns >= 10
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName=NewProcessName, Detail=strcat("WorkerStorm spawns=", tostring(Spawns)), Platform="Windows";
union LinuxOOM, WinIISCrash, WinWorkerStorm
| summarize CrashEvents=count(), arg_min(TimeGenerated, ProcessName, Detail), arg_max(TimeGenerated, ProcessName) by Computer, Platform
| where CrashEvents >= 3
| order by CrashEvents desc
(source:linux.syslog @log.message:*oom-killer* @log.message:(*nginx* OR *httpd* OR *apache2* OR *envoy*)) OR (source:windows.security @EventID:1000 (@Image:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.exe OR *\\nginx.exe OR *\\Nginx.exe OR *\\httpd.exe OR *\\Httpd.exe OR *\\envoy.exe OR *\\Envoy.exe))) OR (source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @NewProcessName:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.exe OR *\\nginx.exe OR *\\Nginx.exe OR *\\httpd.exe OR *\\envoy.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(nginx|httpd|w3wp|envoy|apache2)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName], function=[count(as=spawns), min(_time, as=first_spawn), max(_time, as=last_spawn)])
| spawns >= 10
| storm_window_sec := last_spawn - first_spawn

HazyBeacon Camapign Weaponizes Amazon Web Services for Stealthy Communications

Cyber Security News
2026-06-03 3 use cases 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

A new malware campaign is turning trusted cloud infrastructure against the organizations that rely on it. Known as HazyBeacon and tracked under cluster identifier CL-STA-1020, the campaign targets government networks across Southeast Asia. Rather than using easily blocked servers, the threat actors hide inside one of the world&#8217;s most trusted platforms, Amazon Web Services (AWS). [&#8230;] The post HazyBeacon Camapign Weaponizes Amazon Web Services for Stealthy Communications appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    ( DeviceProcessEvents

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["4931df8650521cfd686782919bda0f376475f9fc5f1fee9d7cf3a4e0d9c73e30", "d20b536c88ecd326f79d7a9180f41a2e47a40fcf2cc6a2b02d68a081c89eaeaa", "304c615f4a8c2c2b36478b693db767d41be998032252c8159cc22c18a65ab498", "f0c9481513156b0cdd216d6dfb53772839438a2215d9c5b895445f418b64b886", "3255798db8936b5b3ae9fed6292413ce20da48131b27394c844ecec186a1e92f", "279e60e77207444c7ec7421e811048267971b0db42f4b4d3e975c7d0af7f511e", "d961aca6c2899cc1495c0e64a29b85aa226f40cf9d42dadc291c4f601d6e27c3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("193.228.128.2") or RemoteUrl has_any ("bestflowers247.online")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["193.228.128.2"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["bestflowers247.online"]);
ImNetworkSession
